articles.title: Mass Effect is Amazon’s next video game adaptation
articles.summary: According to a report from Variety, a tv show based on BioWare’s Mass Effect franchise is officially in development at Amazon MGM Studios.
articles.body: After its success with Fallout and the recently released Like A Dragon: Yakuza show, Mass Effect is the next game Amazon wants to adapt. According to Variety, a show based on BioWare’s military space opera RPG is officially in production at Amazon MGM Studios. Variety has reported that F9: The Fast Saga writer Daniel Casey has signed on to write the show with BioWare producer Mike Gamble serving as executive produce along with Ari Arad. Though BioWare released the Mass Effect Legendary Edition — a collection of the first three games updated for modern consoles — back in 2021, the Mass Effect series hasn’t had an original entry since the release of Mass Effect: Andromeda back in 2017. After Andromeda, BioWare released Anthem, a live-service action game that was significant departure from the studio’s tradition of making single-player, story-driven RPGs. In 2020, BioWare announced that a new Mass Effect game was in-development. News of a Mass Effect TV show comes on what is known as N7 Day, a semi-official, fan-created holiday that celebrates all things Mass Effect. On previous N7 Days, BioWare has teased information about the next game in the series including a trailer that possibly suggested the return of fan-favorite protagonist Commander Shepard whose story ended with the original trilogy. Though no story details have been revealed about the show, it’s a pretty safe bet to guess it’ll focus on the Commander and I personally can’t wait to see her.

articles.title: Moana Review: Dwayne Johnson and Disney Don't Justify Its Own Existence of Their Latest Live-Action Remake
articles.summary: Moana is gorgeous to look at, but it's too faithful to the animated original's storyline (and even camera moves) to offer anything new to the tale. Catherine Laga'aia makes a great bright-eyed protagonist, but Dwayne Johnson can't nail the swaggering demigod Maui's charisma in live-action.
articles.body:
The live-action Moana is the 25th remake of a Disney animated film, arriving only two years after the groundbreaking original film got a sequel. Moana 2 earned far less favourable reviews, but its box office broke a billion dollars, almost double its predecessor's haul. So here we are again, with Disney choosing to copy and paste in the hopes of securing similar financial gain. It probably will, but, as with the rest of Disney’s mixed bag of live-action remakes , Moana begs the question: Just because you can, does it mean you should?

Directed by Broadway's Hamilton and In The Heights director Thomas Kail in his feature debut, this is a beat-by-beat retelling that rarely colors outside the lines. A thousand years after the demigod Maui (Dwayne Johnson reprising the role) stole the heart of the goddess Te Fiti, Moana (Catherine Laga'aia) is chosen by the ocean to find him, and together, return the stone to restore her blighted island Motunui to full health. Same characters, same songs, same hero's journey, which gets quite tedious if, like me, you're a fan of the OG film. It's hard to muster a laugh when you know the punchline for most of the jokes, especially the visual ones regarding Moana's rooster sidekick, Hei Hei, who looks decidedly freaky in CGI.

Still, there's a strong marriage of visual effects and live-action sets, with the vast cinematic scale established early on. Super-wide and sweeping aerial shots capture lush land and golden sand surrounded by a kaleidoscope of blues and greens rippling across the water. The way-finding action sequences, pitting the duo against the crashing waves of the ocean, the mean Minion-esque Kakamora sea pirates and the final boss fire monster Te Kā, are spectacularly realised. Even Maui's musical number "You're Welcome" evokes the playfulness of the animated film as the demigod's tattoo avatars leap off his body and transform into a dance troupe of sand men. It's a fun sequence that evokes the Mary Poppins chalk drawing scene where the soundstage and cartoon characters whimsically collide.

The cast all deliver great vocals, making numbers like "How Far I'll Go" and "We Know The Way" reverberate with emotion. Paired with tribal choreography, conceived by Tiana Nonosina Liufau, who worked on the animated films, and Kayla Fa'amaligi, it's a beautifully resonant display of tradition and culture not often seen in a live-action, mainstream movie. That the entire cast is of Polynesian and Pacific Islander descent is especially admirable and infuses the characters with natural authenticity while also spotlighting new and lesser-known talent.

Laga'aia exudes the earnest, sometimes awkward charm of Moana as she navigates her overprotective dad, gets the hang of her vessel on the open sea, and butts heads with Maui. At times, the direction might have called for her to go bigger with her melancholic feelings, but her scenes with Rena Owen, who plays Moana's cheeky Gramma Tala, are sweetly soulful. John Tui's Chief Tui, Moana's dad, offers a warm regalness. He and Owens might be the closest to accomplishing the spirit of the original characters, but with Laga'aia and Frankie Adams' Sina, Moana's mother, it's easy to believe this is a tight-knit family part of an even tighter-knit community that you want to spend more time with.

The weakest link, unfortunately, is Maui. Johnson's voice performance was memorable in the animated outings, but in embodying the full role, there's a real lack of exuberance, a nonchalance that tempers the flamboyant personality of the arrogant demi-god. It appears to be quite a self-conscious effort, and maybe that is in part due to the god-awful wig they put him in . The director has said that giving Johnson and Laga'aia unruly curls would have played havoc with the CGI and green screen. Still, I'm pretty sure they didn't have curling tongs 2,000 years ago, and that's exactly how these perfectly coiffed hairdos appeared: out of time and jarringly out of place amongst the rest of the cast.

After spending nearly two hours back in this mythical South Pacific world, and to answer that earlier question: No, Moana isn't convincing enough to warrant its existence. But this is where we are in this risk-averse film industry, where we will probably be for a long time, and compared to other live-action Disney remakes, it could be a lot worse.

articles.title: Xbox CEO is reportedly planning three more rounds of job cuts; starting this month, layoffs are part of what CEO Asha Sharma described as 'fundamental reset of how Xbox operates and invests'
articles.summary: Microsoft’s Xbox division is reportedly preparing for three additional rounds of layoffs over the coming months as CEO Asha Sharma pushed ahead with a
articles.body: Microsoft’s Xbox division is reportedly preparing for three additional rounds of layoffs over the coming months as CEO Asha Sharma pushed ahead with a sweeping restructuring aimed at improving the gaming business’ financial performance. According to a report by Fortune, Sharma is planning some more job cuts this month, followed by some additional rounds in November and January, extending a shake-up that has already resulted in thousands of layoffs across Microsoft’s gaming operations. In July this year, Asha Sharman announced plans to eliminate approximately 3,200 jobs during Microsoft's fiscal 2027, including around 1,600 positions that were cut immediately. A further round of layoffs affecting roughly 260 employees followed in September. Microsoft has not publicly confirmed the latest reported plans or disclosed how many employees could be affected.'Fundamental reset' of Xbox operationsThe layoffs are part of what Asha Sharma has previously described as a fundamental reset of how Xbox operates and invests. In a message to employees earlier this year, she said the business was not healthy and acknowledged that Xbox was operating with margins significantly below those of comparable platform and publishing companies.Sharma argued that years of heavy investment in content, hardware, platforms and studio acquisitions had failed to deliver the level of growth Microsoft expected. The restructuring is aimed at simplifying the organisation, reducing costs and focusing resources on projects with stronger commercial prospects.Xbox job cuts: Employees demoralisedSpreading the cuts over several waves has left some employees demoralised, Fortune reports. Some staff feel they are working under a yearlong cloud, waiting to see whether their roles will be next. Fortune also found at least one employee who was laid off and then offered a chance to stay. Some employees appreciated Sharma’s transparency, the report says. Sharma acknowledged the tough decisions but said she values people and does not intend to be transactional.Studios and strategy under reviewThe reset has already resulted in major changes across Microsoft's gaming portfolio. Studios including Double Fine Productions and Compulsion Games have been allowed to regain independence, while other teams have undergone reviews, reorganisations or ownership discussions as Xbox streamlines its operations.The restructuring reflects growing pressure on Microsoft's gaming division to improve profitability amid rising industry costs and a challenging console market. While speculation has emerged over Xbox's long-term future within Microsoft, Sharma recently told media outlets that Xbox is not for sale, while Microsoft executives have publicly backed her leadership of the gaming business.Why Xbox is being resetSharma, 38, took over in February from longtime Xbox head Phil Spencer. She had no video game industry experience, having previously led product work on Microsoft’s AI Foundry platform. Fortune describes Xbox as a roughly $21 billion business with profit margins of about 3 percent, a fraction of what rivals earn and far below what Microsoft expects of its major units. Current Xbox consoles have sold only a little over a third as many units as the PlayStation 5, according to third-party estimates, and memory chip shortages are pushing up hardware costs. Sharma told Fortune in July that Xbox had grown by making many bets and lost focus on its core business, saying the company “spread ourselves too thin.”Questions about Xbox’s futureSeveral current and former staff members told Fortune they believe Xbox is being prepared for a possible sale, spinoff or other restructuring, amid heavy Microsoft spending on artificial intelligence. Judson Althoff, one of Microsoft’s most senior executives, rejected that idea, saying Microsoft would not have put Sharma in charge of a business it intends to sell. articles.title: Fans React to Shrek 2 Remastered's Surprising PC Requirements
articles.summary: Shrek 2 isn’t exactly pushing the bounds of PC graphics, but the recommended specs for the remaster are surprisingly hefty.
articles.body:
Shrek 2 isn’t exactly pushing the bounds of PC graphics, but the recommended specs for the remaster are surprisingly hefty. Originally released in 2004, this remaster boasts better textures, enhanced UI, 4K resolution — and, it seems, a beefy PC.

According to the Steam page , to even run Shrek 2 Remastered you’ll need a GeForce RTX 4060 or RTX 3060 Ti graphics card or equivalent. The developer recommends a GeForce RTX 4070 or RTX 5070 to get the best experience. What have they been feeding him? Have a look at the screenshots in the slideshow, below, to get a sense of what to expect.

“Those swamp graphics better be baller,” said one X / Twitter user . Another complained that they’re able to run Red Dead Redemption 2 at the highest settings, but their PC would apparently struggle with this makeover of a 22-year-old game.

“Seems a bit much for a remaster of a GameCube game but if that’s what we need to render Shrek’s highly detailed green skin then so be it,” said another Twitter user . “They went full in with the GTA 6 aesthetics,” said another .

Other posts expressed concern over it being a “vibe coded” remaster, but there’s currently no AI disclosure on Steam to suggest that’s the case. Valve asked developers to specify when they use AI during game creation or marketing.

Shrek 2 Remastered was revealed alongside a trailer that parodied GTA 6 , and is set to launch just over a week before Rockstar’s behemoth, on November 10. Despite the parody trailer, no one expected it to have similar graphical demands as GTA 6, but here we are. You’ll need 12-16GB of VRAM for this beast. It’s a bit ogre the top.

articles.title: Crimson Desert Charting the Unknown DLC Features Revealed, Including Shipbuilding, Romance, and Housing
articles.summary: Pearl Abyss has pulled back the curtain on the upcoming Crimson Desert DLC, Charting the Unknown, revealing what players can expect. Here's a rundown of all the new features, systems, and mechanics.
articles.body:
Pearl Abyss has pulled back the curtain on the upcoming Crimson Desert DLC, Charting the Unknown, revealing what players can expect.

Charting the Unknown adds new stories, ocean exploration, romance, business management and expanded housing to an already feature-packed Pywel. We have everything you need to know about the major additions below.

There are character focused stories for playable characters Kliff, Damiane, and Oongka, who, having put the fight for the Greymanes and Pywell to bed, set out on new paths. They’ll encounter allies and threats “both old and new.” Based on the new overview video, these new individual character stories will be relatively involved, with cutscenes pushing the plot forward.

The DLC expands the Great Ocean of Pywel area, which you might have crossed in the base game on the back of a dragon. After establishing the Greymane camp, you can unlock shipbuilding, then gather resources to build your own vessel and customize it before you set sail. Pearl Abyss said that you’ll fight enemies (there’s ship combat), establish new strongholds with the Greymanes, and earn new rewards.

You can craft your own dive suit to help you delve deeper into the ocean. “More secrets lie beneath the surface, where new underwater traversal methods let players dive below the waves to uncover sunken ruins, treasure and resources,” Pearl Abyss said, while showing off the ability to hitch a ride on the back of a sea creature.

If you earn the trust of certain characters you can develop romantic relationships and even marry, Pearl Abyss said. One potential romance option is Bari, the Witch of Kindness. Pictures shown reveal a number of dialogue options tied to this mechanic, including "Give a genuine compliment," and "Confess your feelings." “Close” companions may also visit the Greymane Camp to “spend some time together.”

As for housing, you will be able to design the structure of your home from the ground up, including the placement of walls, windows and other structural elements. This sounds fun: once you’ve liberated certain castles, you can claim them and decorate their interiors, turning it into a new home.

In the base game, once the Greymane camp was established, you could send comrades on missions to liberated strongholds. With the DLC, you can manage some of these locations directly. You can now lease facilities across Pywel, assign comrades and equipment, choose which goods to sell, and decide how best to run each business to grow its recognition and profits.

Pearl Abyss said “seasoned fighters seeking a greater test” should consider the new challenge where players face a series of powerful bosses from across Pywel, one after another. If you do well, expect "valuable rewards."

As someone put Crimson Desert down some time ago having sunk over 100 hours into the game, I'm feeling the pull to return to the game for the DLC. Pearl Abyss' relentless pace of updates in the wake of Crimson Desert's launch earlier this year made significant improvements and added game-changing features, but the new systems and mechanics coming with Charting the Unknown clearly take things to a new level. Even if you're not into story side of things, there's plenty to fuss over. The business management system, for example, looks like tens of hours of gameplay alone. Then there's underwater exploration and what I'm sure will end up a fan-favorite: romance.

Crimson Desert Enhanced: Charting the Unknown launches on October 29, 2026 at 2pm PT, 5pm ET, 10pm UK time, on PlayStation 5, Xbox Series X and S, and PC via Steam and the Epic Games Store.

articles.title: Warhammer 40,000: Dawn of War 4 – Detailed Impressions of the Necron and AdMech Factions | IGN Preview
articles.summary: I had a great time getting chromed up with the Adeptus Mechanicus and the Necrons in Warhammer 40,000: Dawn of War 4. The campaign story really starts to come together in some interesting ways in its second chapter. And the ways both of these factions control space differently feel like engaging and welcome additions to the roster compared to the more straightforward playstyle of Orks and Space Marines.
articles.body:
The Adeptus Mechanicus and Necron factions play significantly differently from the previous two we looked at.

The AdMech campaign story features some alluring intrigue.

A few weeks ahead of release, there are still a few technical rough spots.

The Terminator-like Necrons and the cybernetic humans of the Adeptus Mechanicus make a very interesting match-up on the battlefields of Warhammer 40K. At first glance, you might ask yourself why Dawn of War 4 spent two of its faction slots on what could broadly be described as "robot guys." And certainly, they do have some similarities. But now that I've gotten to spend quite a bit of time with both, I can say that they certainly claim their own niches.

While the demo I got to check out also included Space Marines and Orks, those missions were the exact same ones we covered extensively as part of our exclusive IGN First coverage earlier this year. Of course, they've gotten a lot of polish since then. But in terms of the campaign especially, it's a lot of stuff we've already covered. So go check those videos out if you haven't. Because here, I'm going to focus on the stuff that was brand new to me: the AdMech and the Necrons.

We got to see the first six missions of the AdMech campaign, and the tone is quite a bit different from the Orks. While we last left warbosses Guzcutta and Goregutz scrapping over who got to be da biggest boss, not really caring about who got in their way or why, playing as AdMech let me engage with the unfolding events on Kronus much more proactively.

It's the second campaign of the four if you want to go in chronological order, and your choices in the Ork campaign can carry over in certain ways. Whether you chose to elevate the beastboss or the warlord from the stars to power might affect what kinds of Ork enemies you face, for instance. But the Orks play more of a supporting role than anything in these six missions, as the followers of the Omnissiah are focused on the much deeper problem of the Necron presence on Kronus.

Our main hero for the AdMech is Potentia-Delta-9, a technoarchaeologist who often puts the quest for knowledge above the directives of her superiors. She eventually locks dendrites with Sek-Ix-23, a much more by-the-book machine cultist who doesn't appreciate her loose cannon way of doing things. Just like the Ork campaign eventually split off to let you play as Guzcutta or Goregutz, the AdMech story reaches a point where the Magos Dominate of Kronus – the highest-ranking commander of the Mechanicus forces – gives a final ultimatum to Potentia. You can continue playing as her and go rogue, or choose to take over as Sek-Ix and try to restore order.

The story structure is a bit different from the Ork campaign in that it's not actually a branching timeline here. The same story will play out either way, but Potentia's perspective on it is quite different from that of Sek-Ix. They eventually come together before the end, but I don't want to spoil exactly how. I enjoyed this campaign a fair bit more than the Ork one overall. The stakes are higher, the characters are more relatable, and there's some juicy intrigue and ancient secrets to dig into.

The AdMech faction plays very differently from the Orks, as well. They're highly ranged-focused, with basic Skitarii Rangers and Skitarii Vanguards as the backbone of their armies. Both prefer not to get into melee if they can help it. But Vanguards are a bit more durable and excel at medium range, while Rangers file in behind them to lay down fire from a distance. They also get access to Ruststalkers, deadly melee troops who are permanently cloaked until they enter combat or get very close to the enemy.

While these cybernetic humans do a lot of the dirty work, the AdMech specialists come from the higher tech Cult of the Omnissiah. Tracked Kataphron melt through armor with great ease and elite Kastelan Robot maniples transform the frontline into a chrome wall of death in the late game. They're an adaptable army that can get shredded in close quarters if you're not careful, but has tools for almost any situation.

Their buildings form a network called the Noosphere that grows in power the more structures are connected to it, granting bonuses to all structures in the network. This can increase the power of defensive turrets or the production speed of unit structures, for example. But you need either cheap, defenseless Cogitator Relays or more expensive Cognis turrets to link distant structures and resource points to the network, and anything that gets cut off from your main base loses all of the benefits of the Noosphere.

This makes the AdMech somewhat vulnerable to flanking and deep-strike tactics, and creates an interesting strategic question at the start of every match. Should I expand quickly to seize as many points as possible with these fragile, single-path networks? Or should I take it a bit slower and build in redundancies and more automated defenses? Both can work under certain circumstances.

The Necrons have some things in common with the AdMech playstyle, but they're also the most different of the four factions in terms of how their economy works. They are what I sometimes call a "goo faction," in that they want to spread their special kind of goo across the map. Think Zerg creep from Starcraft or Undead blight from Warcraft 3. Their specific goo is a green and black machine lattice that emanates from each Nexus of Dominion, fragile tower structures that also produce their only economic resource: dominion.

Basically, the Necron economy is based on how much of the map area you've managed to blanket in your power grid. This doesn't mean they don't care at all about resource points – capturing them can give powerful secondary benefits like reduced unit costs and increased production speed. But it does mean that they can keep expanding by going around heavily-defended points and gooping up uncontested corners of the map, which is a very interesting way to play.

The theme of the Necron army could be summed up by the declaration, "We are inevitable." Especially at the beginning of a match, they spread very slowly across the map. Swift scarabs are fast enough to seize some control points early, but don't have the staying power to hold them. Meanwhile, your core infantry unit, Necron Warriors, can even stand up to Space Marine Intercessors, but march incredibly slowly.

This makes certain map types that revolve around holding strategic points tricky for Necrons. They have some better fast units later, as well as limited access to teleportation. But against a swarmy faction like Orks, I usually had to resign myself to the fact that they would take an early lead in capture points, and I would simply have to wash over them like a slow-motion tide to wrap up the win decisively in the second half. Knowing when and where to commit is of the highest importance, because after deploying a wave of warriors or teleporting to a strategic location, the Necrons might not have a chance to pivot later.

They were only available in Skirmish, so I didn't get a great idea of what their campaign is about or who their face characters might be. But they're clearly getting set up as the big bads, so I'm interested to learn more about what their motives on Kronus will be.

While what I played is not a final build, I do have to mention some technical issues. There were a couple campaign missions that took upwards of two minutes to load, even on an SSD, and that's kind of unfortunate. Multiple times when a cutscene triggered in the middle of a mission, the entire client would hang for several seconds before proceeding. Hopefully these are all things that can be cleaned up before launch, which is barely over a month away on December 3.

Some technical scuff aside, I had a great time getting chromed up with the Adeptus Mechanicus and the Necrons in Dawn of War 4. The campaign story really starts to come together in some interesting ways in its second chapter. And the ways both of these factions control space differently feel like engaging and welcome additions to the roster compared to the more straightforward playstyle of Orks and Space Marines.

While you're here, check out these recent previews of other big upcoming games we've checked out recently!

Leana Hafer is a contributing freelancer for IGN with a specialty in RPGs, strategy, horror, and survival games. She has been reviewing video games professionally since 2010 and is one of IGN's most prolific contributors, with more than 100 reviews published. articles.title: Stranger Than Heaven: The Final Preview of the Yakuza Team’s Ambitious, Decades-Spanning Action-Adventure
articles.summary: in a new three-hour demo, I got to play Stranger Than Heaven from the start, see a bit of its decade-spanning story in action, and explore the different towns that represent each time period. That also meant getting real familiar with how to throw hands in the re-tuned combat, and it feels like I've done a complete 180-degree turn on RGG Studio's next game. Meaning, I’m now all-in on the Yakuza team’s latest.
articles.body:
It tells a serious story that shows how discrimination of the early 20th century shapes someone, but intentionally includes certain anachronisms.

The parry-based combat mechanics work really well once you lock in with it.

There are some top-tier minigames, including being a music and club manager to fit the theme of music breaking cultural barriers.

I was conflicted coming out of my first hands-on with Stranger Than Heaven earlier this year, generally liking what I saw but unsure if its slower, clunky combat system would get better in time. That was a 45-minute demo that thrust you into battle without any real setup, but in a new three-hour demo, I got to play it from the start, see a bit of its decade-spanning story in action, and explore the different towns that represent each time period while playing all-new minigames that fill the streets. That also meant getting real familiar with how to throw hands in the re-tuned combat, and it feels like I've done a complete 180-degree turn on RGG Studio's next game. Meaning, I’m now all-in on the Yakuza team’s latest.

Stranger Than Heaven's premise drew me from the first reveal – a story about a man of mixed ethnicity in a tumultuous time between Japan and the US, spanning decades and leading into where the Tojo Clan began in 1960s Kamurocho. As someone who's played every Yakuza / Like A Dragon game, this sounds like it could hit hard. Being familiar with the dynamic of being mixed and struggling to find your place in society, it seems like a story that's touching on something very few game stories have.

It starts with lead character Makoto Daito looking to get out of San Francisco in 1915 while fleeing the scene of a crime he did not commit. But the bastard cops pursuing him don't care – they can pin the crime on a "foreigner" and call it a day. And man, it's been a while since I've heard some of these old time-y slurs towards Asians, but that's the tone being set here with regard to the discrimination they faced during this time. Thankfully, we get to whoop their ass as the tutorial for the intricate combat system. He escapes on the last ship leaving the Bay as a stowaway, meets Snoop Dogg's character named Orpheus after tussling with the ship crew, and arrives in the small Japanese town of Kokura.

Here's what I'll say about Orpheus; Snoop Dogg's role kind of works for what this story is doing because part of it seems to be about outcasts finding community through music. One thing director Mikinobu Abe mentioned is that Stranger Than Heaven isn't trying to be time-period accurate – and maybe being anachronistic breaks the believability of its world, but I want to see more of how this is done. They also just kinda let Snoop Dogg do his thing, even teaching Makoto how to roll up loose cigarettes, which is also a gameplay mechanic for crafting cigs that give temporary stat boosts!

Stranger Than Heaven takes on a more serious tone, however. The story sequence I played in Kokura shows Makoto as a very timid outsider whose deep blue eyes give away that he's an outsider – and again, discriminated against in a country he's supposed to be home to. He meets a hostess named Tae at a restaurant under the pretense of getting closer to a crime boss he's tasked with helping take down. The way he clearly lacks the social skills, or just feels shame for who he is, comes across powerfully in these cutscenes. That anxiousness causes him to break since he's compelled to be an honest person, and so they both lay their motives bare.

This made for over 15 minutes of cutscenes, and I was still locked in the entire time. RGG Studio and the Yakuza series have been some of the best in terms of cinematics and actor performances, and Stranger Than Heaven proved that it still has the sauce, letting the intimate details speak volumes and establish a believable dynamic between characters.

The demo fast-forwarded to a raid on a factory in Kokura where Tae was being held captive by said crime boss, so I didn't have any real context for what led up to this moment. However, this is where it dialed in the combat. It still feels pretty sluggish and gets a little messy when dealing with crowds, but the calculated nature of fights shined through. The bumpers control left and right light attacks while the triggers are for respective heavy attacks, which is a great idea on paper, and once I came to grips with the directional parry system, I started flowing through each fight. While holding the guard button, you have to either time the parry with a left or right light attack to stagger your foe – and you really have to pay attention to attack animations not just for timing, but to make the correct call on the direction it's coming from. Stranger Than Heaven joins the crowded ranks of action games with parry systems, yet this seemingly minor mechanic could be the difference in having something more engaging.

Your attacks also change based on the weapon you have equipped. A big odachi sword isn't always the best option even if it's powerful, and the massive hammer is great for breaking guard and finishing enemies with a nasty smack to the face, but it slows down your overall movement. So, I mostly gravitated toward the one-handed knife and wooden club, which gave much-needed mobility and kept me feeling nimble for those directional parries. As I fought through the factory and faced waves of enemies, it kept clicking and it prepared me for the boss fight at the end. Instead of feeling intimidated, I was excited to test whether or not I actually came to grips with the combat system – turns out, I did. Understanding what's parry-able and nailing down dodges around the boss rather than just backing up, also not getting greedy with openings, were the keys to surviving. It's demanding, and I like that about it.

Abe confirmed that RGG Studio reworked the combat after feedback based on the earlier demos, and while it still has its quirks, it has improved drastically from what I played. So, when I got to the snowy town of Kure as the story moves to 1929, I sought out the fight club side activity where I'd just fight dudes in a pit for money. This made Stranger Than Heaven feel like a boxing game, and when I thought of it like that, combat started to make more sense. There are a ton of weapon types to upgrade and gain new techniques from, so I'll be curious to see how this system could evolve over an entire playthrough.

As a game in the Yakuza lineage, you already know that these towns are going to be filled with interesting side activities. The last portion of my demo took place in 1943 Osaka, specifically Sotenbori (real-life Dotonbori), which you may recognize from the Yakuza games. And Stranger Than Heaven might just have RGG's best stuff yet. But first I want to talk about a few of the smaller things I really enjoyed.

This game's got beyblades, man! It's called beigoma and you basically collect spinning tops with different weight distribution and rotational speeds to use in matches. Choose your beigoma, time your power and accuracy on a meter like a golf game, and let it rip! There's also Menko, which is pretty much a game of pogs like we'd do at the school playground as kids. Here, you slam down menko cards to knock others off the table and can use different throwing angles to your advantage.

Of course, every RGG game needs mahjong and I've learned to play recently (shouts out to my homegirl Jackie), opening a whole new way to sink hours into these games without advancing the main story! There are also quicker, one-off things like a shooting gallery for items, five-finger fillet, and arm wrestling.

Most importantly, Stranger Than Heaven fuses the club / business management and karaoke minigames into one robust side activity called Showbiz – and I already love it from what I played. It's thematically coherent with music being one of the major thrusts of the story, and it fits who Makoto becomes as a character. You'll employ musicians, set up props for the stage, set ticket prices, choose the songs they perform, and hopefully draw crowds to make money. It then brings in an easygoing rhythm game element, having you time the transitions for lights and stage effects with the performance to keep the crowd engaged.

It's said to be a consistent throughline as the story spans different decades and eras, and a lens to see how Japan changes in those time periods with fashion, music, and nightlife. And it's how the character Keiko, played by J-pop idol Ado, is woven into the world. As a big-time fan of Ado myself, it's pretty wild hearing her voice a character in a game, but also singing the very songs her character performs. I heard and played two of her in-game songs, both being era-appropriate, and it's such a nice touch where a celebrity casting works really well.

Along with being a music and club manager, you can customize the individual tracks of the songs that are available. So you can take the same old song, change what kind of instrument, mood, or tonality fills the lead, rhythm, bass, or drums tracks to completely change the genre of the song. For example, I basically recreated fourth-wave ska with a classic Balkan brass tune by setting every instrument to "intense" for a contemporary punk sound and setting the horns to "melancholy" – Streetlight Manifesto, eat your hearts out. Again, this is one of the ways things get anachronistic, but damn this is pretty sick.

I find so many parts of Stranger Than Heaven fascinating, and in talking to Yu Shirota, who plays Makoto Daito, he mentioned bring together his careers in music and acting together into one role, but also his own identity as a half-Japanese person who primarily speaks Japanese and still struggled with finding his place in the world. The story encompasses time periods during a tumultuous time in history with Imperial Japan, World War II, and Western culture spilling over, and Abe said that this is a story more about how a man navigates a world that's constantly changing around him.

But then there's the whole digital necromancy of Tupac. RGG studio head Masayoshi Yokoyama already told me earlier this year about how they think using his likeness is a good fit, and talked with Tupac's estate and family about the project to get approval, despite the backlash and overall tastelessness conceptually. Involving Snoop Dogg also seems like stunt-casting, but maybe that could work out well in the end.

Sometimes I don't know what to make of Stranger Than Heaven and I still have reservations about it, despite being one of the upcoming games I'm looking forward to most. And if anything, I just want to see what the hell RGG is doing with some of its questionable parts. But now, its gameplay and story are coming into focus and I need to know how it all plays out in the end. We'll see soon since it's the first major release of 2027, launching on January 15 for PlayStation 5, Xbox Series X|S, and PC.

Be sure to check my full conversation with director Mikinobu Abe and lead actor Yu Shirota where we talk about music, being outsiders, and how all that informs the story of Stranger Than Heaven.

While you're here, check out these recent previews of other big upcoming games we've checked out recently!

Michael is reviews editor at IGN and regularly contributes with previews, interviews, live events coverage, and news all in written and video form. He's usually entrusted with covering long RPGs and tech products, but he's got range when it comes to games. You'll also catch him at conventions and hosting video content, including IGN's weekly podcast Unlocked .

articles.title: Halo Special Edition Xbox Console Hallmark Keepsake Ornament Is Now Available
articles.summary: Hallmark has just released a delightful Keepsake Ornament based on the Halo Special Edition of the original Xbox console that Microsoft released in 2004.
articles.body:
Every year, Hallmark releases hundreds of new Christmas ornaments, including some very cool ones based on video games and geek culture . This year, as an Amazon-exclusive release that just went live, you can get the Xbox Halo Special Edition Console Hallmark Keepsake Ornament ( see it at Amazon ). The ornament is a miniature version of the translucent green Halo-themed special edition Xbox console Microsoft released in 2004. It’s available now for $27.99.

Xbox Halo Special Edition Console - Hallmark Keepsake Ornament

The ornament looks just like a tiny version of the real thing. It has the chunky rectangular console, decked out in translucent green plastic and the words “Halo Special Edition” on the front right. It also has an adorable little cord leading to a similarly green original Xbox controller sitting on the console.

It’s also a “Magic Light and Sound” ornament, meaning it, well, lights up and makes sound. When you press the tiny Power button on the ornament, the light comes on and it plays the console startup sound and music from " Halo Theme Mjolnir Mix " from Halo 2.

Also included are the three Alkaline LR44 button batteries required to make it light up and play music. And the size in inches is 3.5 x 1.25 x 3.5, so it's a small thing (you know, the size of a standard Christmas ornament). I have the SNES Hallmark Keepsake Ornament, and I love it.

Xbox Console - Hallmark Keepsake Ornament

If you’re interested in an original Xbox Christmas ornament but you're not particularly keen on the Halo Special Edition, you can purchase a standard Xbox Hallmark Keepsake Ornament instead ( see it at Amazon ). It debuted in 2024 but is still available and still looks like a perfectly tiny version of Microsoft’s original game console.

Halo UNSC Warthog Hallmark Keepsake Ornament

PlayStation Console Ornament With Light and Sound

Dreamcast Console Hallmark Keepsake Ornament

Link - The Legend of Zelda Hallmark Keepsake Ornament

Alternately, a bunch more gaming ornaments came out this year, including a Halo Warthog, as well as Pokémon, Zelda, and more. Fans of other classic consoles can pick up a rather excellent PS1 ornament , perhaps to complement their PlayStation LEGO set ?

In similar news, Microsoft is releasing a new translucent green version of the Xbox Series X on November 13. However, only 25,000 of these special edition consoles are being made, and it has already sold out everywhere it went up for preorder. You may be able to get one at release, if more stock becomes available.

articles.title: First Permanent Pokémon Store Outside Asia to Open in London by 2029
articles.summary: The first permanent Pokémon store outside Asia will open in London “by 2029.”
articles.body:
The first permanent Pokémon store outside Asia will open in London “by 2029.” The retail space will be open to fans of all ages, with merchandise, community spaces, and “one-of-a-kind experiences.”

According to The Pokémon Company, the store’s opening will kick off a broader rollout of stores across the world. The exact location for the London store hasn’t been announced.

“We are always exploring new opportunities that help us create unique and memorable experiences for our fans,” chief product and experience Officer at The Pokémon Company International, Gaku Susai, said. “This new London store will give visitors the chance to step into the world of Pokémon, whether they’re discovering the brand for the first time or have been Trainers for years.

“We hope it becomes a place where everyone can come together, feel like part of a community and enjoy the magic of Pokémon in a whole new way.”

A previous location opened in New York in 2001, but was closed in 2005 to make way for Nintendo New York, a store with broader Nintendo-based merch. The London store doesn’t have a name yet, but The Pokémon Company avoided calling it a Pokémon Center in its announcement.

The store’s opening is part of a wider expansion by Pokémon in the UK. The Pokémon European International Championships, hosted at London’s Excel Center for the past several years, features its own pop-up Pokémon Center which always sells out fast.

In the world of Pokémon video games, Pokémon Winds and Pokémon Waves (Generation 10) are slated for a global simultaneous release on the Nintendo Switch 2 in 2027.

articles.title: One Piece: Grand Gourmet Often Feels as Shallow as the Lovestruck Chef It's Based Around
articles.summary: Unless you’re an established fan of One Piece and want some fan service, there’s no rush to climb aboard for this culinary voyage.
articles.body:
When it comes to translating One Piece into a video game, developers have typically taken the action route, leaning on flashy battles and wild Devil Fruit powers as pirates sail the high seas. That makes One Piece: Grand Gourmet’s Sanji-centric restaurant builder with the full roster of characters from across the series is an inspired choice. But while I adore the premise and appreciate revisiting the major locations and feeding nearly every character, working to win over residents of the Grand Line often feels as shallow as the lovestruck chef it's based around.

After a storm separates them from the rest of the crew, Sanji and Luffy find a restaurant ship being terrorized by a group of fake Straw Hat pirates who are posing as (and giving a bad name to) the restaurant of Sanji’s mentor, the Baratie. The duo sets sail to beat the fakers in culinary battles and clear the Baratie's name throughout the Grand Line and beyond. Taking a chronological path from the early Romance Dawn days in the East Blue all the way to a taste of the latest arc in the manga and anime, Grand Gourmet is packed with fan service in lieu of a meaningful original story. While I wish there was more meat on the bone, I enjoy Grand Gourmet embracing Sanji’s ethos that everyone who needs food will be fed, and it turns out, everyone the Straw Hats ever met is hungry.

Your floating restaurant starts small and empty, with only a kitchen, a table, and Sanji’s chef skills to cook for hungry customers. Feeding people brings in valuable cash you can use to build out the restaurant with more tables, attractions, and decorations to improve the space's comfort. The more comfortable the accommodations, the happier the customers, and the more they will spend on food. Ironically, comfort is an unfortunate word for this metric. The crimes I must have committed to the concept of interior design have to be the most stressful and sloppy places to attempt to enjoy a meal. I love the idea of building a restaurant that pulls elements from various islands and lets you run wild with the decor, with Sanji cooking delicacies from across the globe, but that tantalizing proposition falls flat in execution.

Each new region brings a set of restaurant fixtures themed to the current story arc you’re sailing through, be that new flooring, lamps, benches, or landscaping. For example, the Thriller Bark set features horror-themed decor, plus a spot to plant the stray zombie friends who accompany the living visitors on the ship. Instead of rewarding you for making an aesthetically pleasing, well-organized dining room, Grand Gourmet doesn’t care about actual comfort. Instead, it incentivizes you to cram every square inch with lamps, benches, and shrubbery to boost stats. Neither Crocodile nor Eustice Kidd ultimately cares what their assigned seat looks like. And because of the limited space and clunky reorganization tools, these areas remained cluttered catastrophes that still somehow made a boatload of money.

Some elements also move beyond the typical restaurant vibe to make the ship a more appealing destination, but they aren’t without their own faults, either. My favorite fantastical attractions are meeting spots for giant sea kings or land crabs, which add cool elements to the ship's deck and showcase the eccentric animal designs of the One Piece world. It’s fun to collect fish to store in an aquarium or keep the pets of visitors in animal-friendly environments. However, once you have the features and creatures in place, there’s not much else to do with them. They’re yet another money-collecting attraction that doesn’t affect their surroundings besides providing a small bump of comfort.

Like the interior design, the restaurant’s food has promising building blocks but lacks the finesse to make planning a proper meal worth the trouble. Sanji draws inspiration from his fellow crewmates and restaurant visitors, letting him make everything from simple dishes like rice or spring rolls to fantastical concoctions based on legendary characters or events from the One Piece world. Piecing together a balanced meal of up to four items lets you sell products at a higher price, and you can increase it further by pairing them with other food endorsed by the same Straw Hat crew member. Except, like the design elements, it’s disappointing that diners are never picky about what you specifically serve them; it only matters that you put the food out.

The best course of action is to serve what’s going to rake in the most cash every time, which the automatic meal tool already does effectively. I wish there were incentives for putting together a regional meal or a group-inspired platter to break up the monotony of only pairing the priciest products. This extends to the fake Baratie boss battles, which put Sanji in a Food Network-esque cooking competition, in which the automatic meals were still plenty successful. You can always put together bespoke plates of food and decorate a meal with different figures, plates, and utensils to spice up the meal-planning experience – there’s just not any reason to do so outside of having a little fun.

Learning to cook new foods is critical to building the restaurant's reputation and fighting fake Baratie, but whether or not you’ll unlock a crucial recipe is a crapshoot. Some foods are key to turning a customer into a fan of the restaurant, which lets them follow you to new regions, but it's nigh impossible to know who might know which recipe. Nothing points you toward who to impress and what food they are capable of inspiring. You have to be lucky enough to have the right items on hand, and the right people on board, to crack a novel recipe. Unlocking a specific food is often dumb luck, and while it can be frustrating to figure out, much of what you need falls into your lap at the right time. The moments when things don’t come together feel bad, though, especially when your favorite characters have to be left behind when the time arrives to move forward on the journey.

While Sanji handles the cooking responsibilities, Luffy sets out to explore with the rest of the pirate crew. The action itself is simple, but I looked forward to searching each new region because it’s one of the few tasks that enables the restaurant to consistently flourish in meaningful ways. These idle activities cost Berry, affinity points, or coins to send the crew to important One Piece islands, villages, and bases – the price is worth it, though, as exploration rewards you with new faces to visit the restaurant, giftable items to create new fans or increase profitability, and precious ingredients for new kitchen concoctions. Some rewards are level-gated while others require a specific crew member to bring them home, giving me a great reason to level up every member of the Straw Hat crew whenever possible (once you’ve found them somewhere in the vast ocean, that is).

Each crew member helps out the restaurant in a way only they can, and these are some of the best realized parts of Grand Gourmet. Sanji, of course, cooks all of the meals; Franky, the shipwright, creates new furnishings and can expand the square footage of the ship; crafty Ussop makes decorations and utensils to modify meals; and the swordsman Zoro trains the Straw Hats, allowing them to level up further for expeditions and other activities. My favorite crew member is the money-hungry Nami, who not only bailed me out financially multiple times but also negotiates a half-price discount on new amenities once a day, giving me a neat loophole to buy expensive ship upgrades on the cheap. Every member of the pirate crew brings a fun element to the ship, even if everything doesn’t necessarily help the cause of beating the fake Baratie.

Running a business isn’t cheap, especially when serving hundreds of hungry mouths in the middle of the briney deep, but I’m disappointed by the lack of pressure or punishment for spending far outside my means. Every shop, buffet, and employee hired to help the cause has daily overhead, which put me deep in financial trouble almost every day. (Don’t get me started on how much it was to add Blackbeard to the payroll.) Each sunrise, my Berry count went negative, and I had to crawl through the day. Because no friction challenged my poor financial management, I never needed to find a better way to run the company. The only time anyone cares how shallow my pockets are is when I'm spending money during the day, and even then, someone usually bailed me out immediately, filling my coffers far more than necessary.

With no reason to think too hard about the business management side of things, what has instead kept me playing Grand Gourmet (even after the close to 20 hours it took me to roll credits) is seeing damn near every single named One Piece character running around the ship and interacting with each other. It’s fun to see old comrades share a table or bitter rivals chat about characters they relate to. Some meetups are surprising and funny, like two villains discussing “work,” which may or may not involve poisoning people with synthetic Devil Fruits. There are also references to its own lack continuity, which make for interesting meetups between characters who may not exist in the same place or lifetime.

Each character has an affection rating that, when raised to a specified level, can give your staff new items to craft or more customers to invite, making them important to interact with beyond just the fun of having them aboard. Grand Gourmet looks great too, full of small details on the hundreds of character sprites that are truly impressive. Almost every character’s design is recognizable and unique, with many featuring special animations that bring each person to life, like Akainu firing up a giant magma fist while helping to create a new dish. These flourishes don’t happen often, but do inject some much-needed panache to the normally mundane way everyone strolls around.

While almost every character the anime has produced is here, it’s a shame the same can’t be said for the memorable music, voice cast, or sound effects from its long history. Instead, the soundtrack is limited to a handful of nondescript background themes on a short loop paired with a painfully small sample of sound effects, which makes it feel like an early iOS game (which isn’t a huge shock given this game is so deeply tied to developer Kairosoft’s mobile game lineage). A big part of One Piece’s appeal lies in its audio design and music, so it’s a bummer that Grand Gourmet has none of that.

articles.title: Fallout Day Continues: The World of Fallout Museum Exhibit Expands, Choose the Flavor of Nuka Twist, and More
articles.summary: As part of the ongoing Fallout Day celebrations, Bethesda has revealed new Fallout partnerships in the real world.
articles.body:
As part of the ongoing Fallout Day celebrations, Bethesda has revealed new Fallout partnerships in the real world.

The highlight for me is the expansion of the World of Fallout exhibit at the National Atomic Testing Museum in Las Vegas. This includes a collection of props, costumes, and memorabilia from the games and the Amazon TV show. The update will introduce two new galleries, doubling its footprint and featuring interactive installations, museum artifacts, and interpretive displays. Check out pictures of the exhibit in the slideshow below:

The World of Fallout Exhibit at the National Atomic Testing Museum Photos

Across the globe, the Fallout Cafe returns to Tower Records in Tokyo for a second year, offering Fallout-themed food and exclusive merchandise. We’ve got images of what to expect if you can make your way to Japan for a visit. Images including of the menu are below:

Back on home soil, the third annual Fallout Night with the Texas Stars is set for October 24. Fans who attend can receive a collectible Fallout bobblehead.

And finally — and perhaps most importantly! — Bethesda and Jones Soda’s next collaboration is Project T.W.I.S.T. (Taste-worthiness Initiative for Shelter Transition), which invites fans to help choose the flavor of Nuka Twist. This is important because the flavor of Nuka Twist has not yet been established in game content. Voting takes place on the Jones Soda website October 21-31.

Nuka-Twist was added to Fallout 76 as a Nuka-Cola variant consumable as part of the Nuka-World on Tour update. Drinking it gets you a 10 minute, +2 buff of one of your 7 S.P.E.C.I.A.L. stats, so it’s pretty handy. Watch out for those +5 rads, though.

Already this week, Bethesda has shown off three eye-catching mods for Fallout 4 , one of which launched yesterday, October 20. Fallout Day itself is this Friday, October 23 (October 23, 2077 is of course the day in the Fallout timeline the bombs fell, sparking The Great War that caused the irradiated wasteland fans of the franchise have been playing in over the last few decades).

Fallout’s 30th anniversary arrives next year, so expect some big announcements from Bethesda then. What’s it working on? It’s got everything from Fallout 3 and New Vegas remasters to Fallout 5, with an Obsidian-developed Fallout spinoff in there somewhere. Work continues on Fallout 76 and Fallout Shelter, and Season 3 of the Fallout TV series is also incoming. In short, Microsoft is doubling down on Fallout, with new Xbox boss Asha Sharma striving for increased profitability.

articles.title: Oni Press Reveals New Adventure Time: Fionna & Cake Spinoff Series
articles.summary: If you prefer Fionna and Cake to Finn and Jake, then Oni Press has just the Adventure Time spinoff series for you.
articles.body:
We all love a good Adventure Time story, but sometimes it's nice when Finn and Jake take a backseat in favor of their gender-swapped, alternate-universe counterparts, Fionna and Cake. That's why we're pleased to see Oni Press giving that Dynamic Duo their own series.

Adventure Time: Fionna & Cake #1 Cover Art Gallery

articles.title: Exclusive — See 7 New Cards From Magic: The Gathering Star Trek, Including 1 That Remembers the Most Iconic Drink of TNG
articles.summary: Magic: The Gathering: Star Trek is the card game's final frontier of 2026, and while Wizards of the Coast revealed quite a few of the cards yesterday, IGN today has seven cards we can exclusively reveal ahead of the November 13 release date.
articles.body:
Magic: The Gathering: Star Trek is the card game's final frontier of 2026, and while Wizards of the Coast revealed quite a few of the cards yesterday, IGN today has seven cards we can exclusively reveal ahead of the November 13 release date.

Just like the Marvel Superheroes set that came out earlier this year, Magic: The Gathering Star Trek has cards from pretty much every era of the show's history. Even the small selection of cards we have here covers everything from the original series to Deep Space 9 and Lower Decks.

We're revealing seven exclusive Magic: The Gathering Star Trek cards:

The star of the show is a common artifact called 'Tea, Earl Grey, Hot.' Really, the reason why this card is noteworthy is because of the reference to Captain Picard's hot beverage of choice, but in the right deck, it could do some work. It's simply a 2 mana artifact with the 'Food' subtype, which automatically makes it useful in some decks.

Magic the Gathering: Star Trek – IGN Exclusive Card Reveals

But unlike the Food Tokens we've all made hundreds of, this one nets you a card when it enters. When you sacrifice it, you can either gain 3 life like any other Food Token, or you can have it deal 2 damage to an opponent. Finally, I can just throw tea in someone's face.

The more mechanically interesting card is Mirror Universe Intrusion. It's a sorcery for a colorless, a blue and a black, that lets you create a copy of a creature an opponent controls, only it has menace. That's a flavor win, but something that you can do with countless other cards.

However, if you pay the kicker of 4 colorless, a blue and a black, you instead copy all of your opponent's creatures, and give them all menace. At nine mana, it's quite an investment, but a good way to essentially steal an opponent's board.

Mirror Universe Intrusion also has a couple of 'booster fun' treatments, with a borderless version and the new showcase treatment that loos like it came right out of a Star Trek box set.

Magic: The Gathering | Star Trek Play Booster Box

Magic: The Gathering | Star Trek Collector Booster Box

Magic: The Gathering | Star Trek Beam Me Up Bundle

Magic: The Gathering | Star Trek Scene Box - Divergent Timeline

Magic: The Gathering | Star Trek Scene Box - Enterprise-Q

Magic: The Gathering | Star Trek Beginner Box

Magic: The Gathering | Star Trek Commander Deck - Federation Fleet

Magic: The Gathering | Star Trek Commander Deck - Landing Party

Magic: The Gathering | Star Trek Commander Deck - Klingon Fury

Magic: The Gathering | Star Trek Commander Deck - We are the Borg

Magic: The Gathering | Star Trek Commander Deck Bundle

Magic: The Gathering | Star Trek Collector's Edition Commander Deck Bundle

Magic: The Gathering | Star Trek Draft Night

Dahar Master is a 4-mana 4/3 at common, and with its ability to sacrifice a nonland permanant to shock any target, should be useful at your prerelease. But it's kind of one of those cards that's going to end up populating a bulk box the day after you open it in a pack.

Unexplored Wilds is interesting, becuase it's an effect we've seen countless times with cards like Evolving Wilds, but worse. You can tap it for a colorless mana, unlike Evolving Wilds, but if you want to sacrifice it to tutor up a basic land, you need to spend one mana to do it, which is bad. Just like Dahar Master, this will probably be useful in draft to help you color fix, but it's going to end up in your bulk box the moment you get home.

This new Star Trek set is shaping up to at least be the most interesting Universes Beyond set of the year so far, and I am interested to see how some of the artifact strategies play out across different formats. This set is also getting previewed after Wizards of the Coast revealed Darkhold Destiny at an NYCC panel , which takes a Universes Beyond property and creates a wholly original story.

articles.title: Everything Coming to Cyberpunk 2077 With the 2.5 Update, Including New Side Quests, New Double Trouble Perk, and Much More
articles.summary: CD Projekt has revealed what to expect from the Cyberpunk 2077 2.5 update, which ties in with the release of Netflix anime Edgerunners 2. Check out the patch notes.
articles.body:
CD Projekt has revealed what to expect from the Cyberpunk 2077 2.5 update, which ties in with the release of Netflix anime Edgerunners 2 .

Edgerunners content includes a new side quest called Clampdown, which is set before the events of Edgerunners 2 ( CD Projekt recently confirmed that Edgerunners 2 is set in 2078 , just one year after the game itself). During this quest you’ll get a new 5-piece gear set based on the character King from Season 2. There’s also a new radio station that has tracks from the Edgerunners series.

But there’s plenty more coming with 2.5 unrelated to Edgerunners, including more side quests. The Welcome to Paradise! side quest takes you on a journey to uncover a mystery and explore Night City on a guided tour narrated by Richard Night, the founder of Night City itself. There’s also a new side quest that acts as an extension of Fool on the Hill, which includes new tarot cards.

Meanwhile, 2.5 lets you customize your hand cyberware, which will let you give your Mantis Blades, Gorilla Arms, Monowire or Projectile Launch System implants a new look. Each Glamdoc is located in a unique shop, along with their own intro scene with voiceover and animations, and offers a unique catalog of cyberware skins with customizable colors.

Perhaps the most significant addition with 2.5 is the new Double Trouble perk in the Cool tree, which lets you dual-wield Pistols and Revolvers from the Power category for the first time. The hope is that the perk will enable an entirely new playstyle, and I’m sure fans will get a kick out of trying it out.

Elsewhere, there’s cross-platform mod support on PC, Mac, PlayStation 5, PlayStation 5 Pro and Xbox Series X and S, and various quality-of-life improvements, such as saves in the “Load Game” menu grouped by separate playthroughs, and, finally, an FOV (Field Of View) slider on consoles.

On the tech side of things, there’s support for DLSS 4.5, including up to 6X Multi Frame Generation or Dynamic Multi Frame Generation, and the 2nd Generation Transformer Model, and various performance improvements.

Every CD Projekt Red Game In Development

Overall, 2.5 is a welcome surprise for Cyberpunk 2077, after CD Projekt had indicated it had no plans for further DLC for the hugely successful game. Of course, The Witcher 3 is getting a new expansion 12 years after launch, so perhaps CD Projekt will return later on with a new expansion for Cyberpunk 2077. For now, though, 2.5 is sure to spark a return to Night City for lapsed players, and give fans of Edgerunners a push to jump in if they haven’t already.

Added a new side quest, Clampdown , set before the events of Cyberpunk: Edgerunners 2 . To unlock it, complete The Heist and two gigs for Wakako, then wait for a message from her.

Added a new 5-piece gear set based on the character King, which can be obtained during the Clampdown side quest.

Added a new radio station, HKGN 102.0 FM, featuring a selection of tracks from the Cyberpunk: Edgerunners series.

A brand-new clothing collection has arrived in Night City! 5 new outfit sets can now be purchased from certain clothing vendors:

Maxiwear: available in Heywood, Arroyo, Little China

NetWatch: available in Kabuki, Japantown

IconAmerica: available in Pacifica, Badlands, Northside

And one more set that will hit Night City shelves just a little later...

The NUS Infiltrator clothing set can be now purchased from clothing vendors in Kabuki and Japantown.

4 new TWINTONE skins for Quadra Turbo-R V-Tech are now available via Twitch Drops.

Some of the hairstyles that were previously exclusive to NPCs are now available for V. Please note that some hairstyles are available only to feminine or masculine body types.

Show off your chrome! You can now customize your hand cyberware. Equip your Mantis Blades, Gorilla Arms, Monowire or Projectile Launch System, and visit one of 5 Glamdocs (marked with a spray paint icon on the map) to give your implants a fresh, new look. Each Glamdoc is located in a unique shop, along with their own intro scene with voiceover and animations, and offers a unique catalog of cyberware skins with customizable colors.

Sometimes one gun just isn't enough. The new Double Trouble perk in the Cool tree (along with four auxiliary perks) introduces an entirely new playstyle, allowing you to dual-wield Pistols and Revolvers from the Power category.

Added frames from the Cyberpunk Trading Card Game to Photo Mode, allowing you to make your preem shots look like custom cards.

Added new poses in Photo Mode to show off your dual-wielding prowess.

Added Cross-Platform Mod Support, powered by mod.io, a first step into cross-platform modding that allows you to easily browse and install a selection of player-created mods directly from the in-game menu. More mods will become available over time. The feature is available on PC, Mac, PlayStation 5, PlayStation 5 Pro and Xbox Series X|S.

Welcome to Paradise ! Added a new side quest that takes you on a journey to uncover a mystery and explore Night City on a guided tour narrated by Richard Night. It unlocks after completing The Heist and reaching level 15 Street Cred.

Added 12 new Minor Arcana Tarot Cards to discover across Night City. The Tarot menu now has separate sections for Major and Minor Arcana. The new tarot cards are part of a new side quest, an extension of Fool on the Hill , which activates after scanning any of the new cards. Collect them all to get a special reward.

Saves in the “Load Game” menu are now grouped by separate playthroughs.

Added item filters to apartment and vehicle stashes.

Modded saves in the "Load Game" menu are now marked with a dedicated icon. Please note that achievements and trophies cannot be earned while playing on console from a modded save file.

Added an FOV (Field Of View) slider on consoles.

Updated the selection of AMD FSR options. FSR 3 upscaling is no longer included, while FSR 2.1, FSR 4, and FSR 3.1 Frame Generation remain available.

Updated the CD PROJEKT RED Account connection, My Rewards and telemetry consent menus.

Added support for DLSS 4.5, including up to 6X Multi Frame Generation or Dynamic Multi Frame Generation, and the 2nd Generation Transformer Model.

Added support for glasses-free 3D effects on compatible Samsung Odyssey 3D monitors, along with a Motion Comfort setting that lets you balance 3D depth and viewing comfort.

Added support for MetalFX Frame Interpolation and Denoising on Mac.

Added a toggle in settings for FSR Anti-Lag 2.

Introduced various performance optimizations, including improvements specifically for Ray Tracing and for PlayStation 5 Pro.

Improved HDR rendering to provide more accurate colors, brightness, and contrast on compatible displays.

Fixed an issue on Nintendo Switch 2 where saving the game could result in a "Save failed - insufficient space" error.

Fixed an issue where adjusting HDR settings on PlayStation 5 had no effect.

Things Done Changed - Fixed an issue where the Delamain cab could get stuck after crashing into another vehicle, blocking quest progression.

Fixed an issue where enabling Film Grain had no effect.

Fixed an issue where tagging enemies while scanning could also cause V to crouch or stand up when using certain control schemes.

Fixed an issue where controller settings for the Third-Person Camera were missing.

Fixed several typos in various languages.

Added various other fixes for features and content introduced since Patch 2.1.

articles.title: Best Buy Is Selling Pokémon TCG: Prismatic Evolutions ETBs at MSRP — But You'll Need An Invite
articles.summary: Best Buy is offering Pokémon TCG: Prismatic Evolutions ETBs for $49.99, around 62% below market price. Here's how to request an invite.
articles.body:
In a world where market price has become the new MSRP for the Pokémon Trading Card Game , you can now score one of its rarest modern ETBs — Prismatic Evolutions — for only $49.99 at Best Buy , thanks to the retailer’s new invite-only listing.

Amazon’s invite-only listings for Pokémon TCG Elite Trainer Boxes and bundles have been one of the best ways to score trading cards at MSRP without having to check multiple in-person retail stores or trying to beat scalper-bots during online drops. However, their now-huge popularity has made the odds of getting one of those said invites a ‘once in a blue moon’ sort of opportunity these days.

Pokemon TCG: Prismatic Evolutions Elite Trainer Box

Seeing that obvious growing issue in the retailer market, that’s likely why Best Buy has been launching sales events like this itself. Instead of paying around $130.50 for a Prismatic Evolutions Elite Trainer Box (its current market price on TCGplayer ), you can pay around 62% less if you’re lucky enough.

Said luck is still the most important factor of all here, though, as that essentially determines if you’ll be able to get one of these Pokémon ETBs for yourself.

First, you’ll need a Best Buy account, and you’ll need to be signed in as you select the “Ask for an invite” button on the page.

In the same way as Amazon’s Pokémon invites go out, your invite request will be kept on Best Buy’s system to be in consideration for the next (or future) stock drops the retailer gets for this particular ETB — before randomly selecting who amongst those requesters actually get an invite.

If you do get selected, of which you’ll be notified by email, you’ll have 24 hours to purchase your Prismatic Evolutions ETB before said invite expires. In light of that fairly narrow window, that’s also why Best Buy advises you to download and use the Best Buy app as well, so you can get real-time alert notifications, as well.

Whilst this all means requesting an invite doesn’t guarantee you’ll get selected this time, you’ll at least stay on the list for any future restocks, too, so you don’t need to request one again each time.

As for what you can get when you finally get an invite, the standard Prismatic Evolutions Elite Trainer Box includes nine Prismatic Evolutions booster packs, an exclusive full-art foil Eevee promo card, 65 Eevee-themed sleeves, 45 Energy cards, dice, condition markers, a player's guide, and a collector's storage box.

articles.title: Avengers: Armageddon Ending Explained - How the Series Teases a Sequel to One of Marvel's Most Infamous Storylines
articles.summary: Avengers: Armageddon ends with a tease that Marvel is finally ready to follow up on its most controversial storyline of the 21st Century. Here's what you need to know.
articles.body:
Full spoilers for Avengers: Armageddon #5, which is available digitally and in comic shops now.

Marvel has released the fifth and final chapter of Avengers: Armageddon, and as promised, there are some big changes hitting the Marvel Universe . As the dust of a tragic battle settles, new alliances are forged, and a new team of Earth's Mightiest heroes begins to take shape . But that's nothing compared to a tease suggesting that Marvel is finally ready to confront one of its most controversial storytelling decisions of the 21st Century.

Read on for a full breakdown of what happens in the Armageddon finale and how this series lays the foundation for Chip Zdarsky and Marco Checchetto's relaunched Avengers comic.

In what is easily the biggest development in Avengers: Armageddon #5, it's strongly hinted that Marvel is finally ready to do what Spider-Man fans have been begging for for almost 20 years now. They seem finally ready to address the controversy surrounding 2007's Spider-Man: One More Day and the Faustian bargain Peter Parker made with Mephisto.

For those not familiar with One More Day, that storyline served as a way for Marvel to finally erase Peter and Mary Jane's marriage (a plot point many creators and editors have complained ages up the character and presents storytelling limitations). In that story, Aunt May is mortally wounded by an assassin's bullet meant for Spider-Man himself. A guilt-stricken Peter agrees to sacrifice his marriage in exchange for May's life. To Mephisto, snuffing out something beautiful and wholesome is even better than claiming a soul.

Marvel used One More Day as a way of returning Peter to a more classical status quo as a struggling bachelor. Needless to say, many fans were unhappy with the idea of their beloved hero making a literal deal with the devil, and the controversy surronding that decision remains two decades later.

Marvel has mostly ignored the controversy in the years since. But if Armageddon #5 is any indication, they may finally be acknowledging Peter's controversial choice and once again pitting Spider-Man against Mephisto. Near the end of this issue, Tony Stark tracks down Doctor Doom's What-If Machine, a device that can generate pocket universes and allow the observer to see how reality will play out when certain decisions are made. Tony asks the machine to show him what will happen if the Avengers keep operating as they have. The machine shows him an image of a sword-wielding Mephisto towering over a battered Spidey.

This image seems to be connected to a teaser Marvel released at NYCC 2026. The teaser featured a montage of recent and upcoming comic book covers juxtaposed with the words "1 Day" and the tagline "Tomorrow Is One Day Away." Readers had already begun speculating that this teaser was alluding to a One More Day follow-up, and now paired with the reveal in Avengers: Armageddon #5, it's really starting to look like Marvel is planning a full-fledged sequel to that infamous comic.

The question is what will come of this latest development. Will Peter be made to remember the bargain he made with Mephisto? Will he remember that he lost not just his wife, but their unborn daughter as well? Will this result in Peter and MJ finally getting back together? We'll find out when this mysterious 1 Day project materializes in June 2027.

Acknowledging One More Day isn't the only example of Avengers: Armageddon reviving years-old plot points. Issue #4 featured the long overdue introduction of Miracleman to the Marvel Universe . David Colton, the post-9/11 Captain America who gained godlike new abilities from an Origin Box, was transformed again when he spoke the magic word "Kimota!" and became Miracleman.

Miracleman turned out to be the sixth, previously unrevealed member of Zdarsky and Checchetto's Avengers roster. The team can clearly use the muscle, as most of the other members are strictly street-level heroes like Daredevil, Wolverine, Luke Cage, and Spider-Man. And even Captain Marvel has seen better days, as her powers have been severely weakened after attempting to absorb the nuclear blast created by Red Hulk.

But issue #5 makes it clear that there are more twists and turns to come on the Miracleman front. The finale reminds us that Colton isn't technically the Marvel Universe's version of Miracleman. The Origin Box that contained his powers came from the Ultimate Universe, where that world's version of Mickey Moran was robbed of his chance to become a hero.

Mister Fantastic reminds Tony of that fact. All of the other Origin Boxes recovered so far correspond to existing, known heroes in the Marvel Universe, but not Colton's. That means there's someone on Earth-616 with these same powers, someone who hasn't made their presence known. The Marvel Universe presumably has its own Mickey Moran, meaning there are actually two Miraclemen in the same world. And somehow, we doubt Earth is big enough for the two of them.

Apart from the aforementioned One More Day 2.0 tease, easily the biggest outcome of Avengers: Armageddon is that the superhero community is in a bad place. World governments were already feeling mistrustful of superhumans in the aftermath of 2025's One World Under Doom crossover, and the events of this story have only exacerbated the situation. By the end of Armageddon, thousands of Russian civilians are dead, and the UN responds by voting on new measures to rein in unlicensed superhumans.

The end result of this is that SHIELD has been reconstituted under Nick Fury, Jr. Fury now has a mandate to protect the world from rogue superhumans. The only country that abstains from voting is the US, which also happens to be the home to 80% of the world's superhumans. As Invisible Woman's contact explains, the government is simply too afraid of the Avengers, Fantastic Four, and others to risk poking the bear. But that may well change as Fury consolidates power.

The political climate of the Marvel Universe is once again similar to that of 2006's Civil War. The US hasn't instituted a new Superhuman Registration Act (not yet), but the public is more fearful and mistrustful of superheroes than they have been in a long time. It's going to make things a lot harder for the new Avengers team, especially if they're called upon to operate outside of US borders.

But there's one final wrinkle as Avengers: Armageddon wraps. In issue #4, Bucky Barnes was believed to be among the thousands killed when Red Hulk detonated in Russia. But issue #5 closes with a scene of Bucky's corpse somehow regenerating and resurrecting. Bucky is then approached by none other than Nick Fury, Sr. The elder Fury informs his old friend that the time has come for them to save the world. It seems father and son will be at odds going forward, as both spymasters believe they're operating in the best interests of the world at large.

What do you think of Avengers: Armageddon's dramatic ending? Are you excited for the new Avengers series and the mysterious 1 Day event? Let us know your thoughts in the comments below.
